title: Five Mexicans arrested in Nigeria over $227m meth lab
html:
Nearly seven tonnes of chemicals used to manufacture meth as well as industrial equipment were also seized

  • Published

Five Mexican nationals and a Nigerian businessman have been arrested in Nigeria after authorities uncovered an industrial-scale methamphetamine laboratory, the country's drug enforcement agency says.

More than 1.5 tonnes of the highly addictive synthetic drug, commonly known as meth, was seized from the facility in the south-eastern state of Enugu. The haul included both finished drugs and meth still being produced.

The National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) estimates the drugs are worth $227m (£173m).

It is the fourth industrial-scale meth laboratory with alleged links to Mexican drug cartels to have been discovered in Nigeria in recent months.

Earlier this year, Nigerian authorities uncovered similar laboratories in Ogun, Oyo and Ebonyi states

The Nigerian businessman, 63-year-old Chuks Enoch Ezeike, also known as "Over Size", is accused of setting up the laboratory and smuggling the five Mexicans into the country using forged Argentine, Colombian and Chilean passports.

The NDLEA identified the five as Oscar Ramos-Cardenas, who it described as the alleged leader of the group, Juan Antonio Sarabia-Cabrera, Luis Enrique Garcia-Amador, Jose Alejandro Renteria-Reyes and Salomon Cabanillas-Torres.

The laboratory, situated behind an oil company in Enugu, also had accommodation for the Mexican nationals, allowing them to live and work there without attracting attention, the agency said.

Speaking at a news conference in the capital, Abuja, on Wednesday, NDLEA chief Mohamed Buba Marwa said the arrests followed a seven-month investigation involving several countries.

The agency had been monitoring Ezeike since April, when it received intelligence allegedly linking him to Ramos-Cardenas, a Mexican national suspected of specialising in large-scale meth production.

In August, the five Mexicans were refused entry into Nigeria after arriving at Abuja's international airport and were sent back to Mexico.

But less than a month later, they tried again, travelling through Colombia and France before arriving in neighbouring Benin, where they were allegedly given forged passports.

This time, Nigerian authorities deliberately allowed them into the country, Marwa said.

"We wanted the whole network: the meth specialist, the financier, the factory and the product. Sending them home a second time would only have postponed the problem," he said.

The men were allegedly met by Ezeike in Lagos before being taken to Enugu, where they were kept under surveillance.

More than 200 anti-narcotics officers were deployed on 11 November to raid the laboratory and a hotel where Ezeike was staying in simultaneous operations.

The five Mexicans were arrested while producing the drug, the agency said. Ezeike told investigators they had been due to leave Nigeria two days later.

Nearly seven tonnes of chemicals used to manufacture meth, as well as industrial equipment, were also seized.

The arrests come amid growing concerns about Mexican drug cartels setting up production bases in West Africa

The NDLEA said Ezeike had admitted owning the laboratory and bringing the Mexican nationals into Nigeria to produce the drug.

Investigators believe the operation was part of a wider international criminal network in which a Mexican cartel recruited and paid specialists to manufacture meth, while Nigerian collaborators allegedly provided the facilities and resources.

The agency has not identified the Mexican cartel it suspects was involved or said whether the six suspects have been formally charged.

The arrests come amid growing concerns about Mexican drug cartels setting up production bases in West Africa, a region long used as a transit route for illicit drugs.

While some of the meth produced in the region supplies a growing local market, traffickers also target lucrative overseas markets, particularly in Europe and Asia.

Earlier this year, Nigerian authorities uncovered similar laboratories in Ogun, Oyo and Ebonyi states.

The latest operation brings to 10 the number of suspected Mexican meth production specialists arrested in Nigeria in recent months, according to the NDLEA. Five others arrested in earlier operations are already in custody awaiting trial.

Issuing a warning to foreign drug cartels, Marwa said: "Nigeria is not your laboratory. It is not your warehouse, and it is not your transit route."
